newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - EU celebrates 40 years of increasing ties.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EU celebrates 40 years of increasing ties.

text.p: When European Union foreign ministers gather next Tuesday to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the Treaty of Rome, they are likely to hail peace as the organisation's greatest achievement.
The representatives of six European countries who met in the Italian capital on March 25, 1957 pledged to lower trade barriers, share farm policy, and abolish obstacles to free movement.
But there was more on the agenda.
Of those present, Italy and Germany had been defeated in war, while Luxembourg, France, the Netherlands and Belgium had been overrun by the enemy.
All had been devastated, and none wanted to take up arms against each other again. Tie us together economically, they argued, and we'll no longer be able to destroy each other.
Political union, too, was on the cards, if not on the table.
"We have great tasks before us...but I rejoice in this great step towards European unification," German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer, the only head of government present, said at the signing ceremony.
From Finland's Arctic villages to Spain's Moorish castles, today's battles are fought in the European Parliament or by veto in the EU's Council of Ministers.
Diplomatic fury no longer erupts over national boundaries and antagonistic political systems, but over farm subsidies and fish quotas.

"Over 40 years, our countries have learned to work together," European Commission President Jacques Santer said in a recent speech. "The time has long passed when a diplomatic dispute...could spark war between two European countries."
HOW EUROPE HAS CHANGED
Loved or loathed by its 350 million citizens, today's European Union bears little resemblence to the European Economic Community created four decades ago.
It has grown from the six in Rome in 1957 to the 15 that will assemble in the city on Tuesday.
Britain -- disdainful of the project when it began -- eventually joined in 1973 along with Ireland and Denmark.

After kicking out their dictatorships, Greece entered in 1981, followed by Spain and Portugal in 1986. Austria, Finland and Sweden rounded off the group in 1996. East Germany became a de facto member by way of re-unification.
The early foray into creating a common market has transcended into a vast single market with no internal tariffs and ever-decreasing obstacles to the free movement of goods and people.
Citizens of the bloc, most carrying EU passports, can work where they like within it.
On the international stage, the European Union speaks with one voice on trade matters, allowing the 15 countries to rival the United States in influence as a trading power.
Tentative steps have also been taken to create a joint foreign policy and common procedures for dealing with crime, immigration and other justice and home affairs matters.
ECONOMIC UNION AND SINGLE CURRENCY
Overshadowing it all is the bloc's most ambitious project to date, economic union and the creation of a single currency by the beginning of 1999.

Although difficulties abound and it is by no means certain how many countries will qualify to adopt it, mainstream Europeans say there is huge political will on the part of France and Germany, the EU powerbrokers, to see it through.
All these achievements -- though rejected in some quarters as steps along the road to a European super-state -- have made EU membership a passionate goal of many of those outside.

Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Latvia, Romania, Bulgaria, Estonia, Lithuania, Cyprus and Turkey are all eager to join. All but Turkey has been given a clear promise that they eventually will.
Others, such as Croatia and Bosnia, are in the wings, although decades away from having any real chance of being accepted.

Such a richness of candidates brings with it problems never considered by the founding fathers who sat together in the 1950s to design institutions and procedures for six economically advanced western European countries.
The prospect has forced the EU to draft a new treaty, one it says boldly will take it into the 21st century.
But bickering over issues such as national sovereignty have severely limited the scope of the treaty, which is due to be completed by June.

Foreign ministers plan to take advantage of the Rome celebrations to discuss the state of the treaty negotiations, now seen as less a preparation for new members -- some of which may be in within five years or so -- than fine-tuning.
